captions.text: The canteen has a list of snack votes, but “apple” and “Apple” appear as different choices.
Will the graph tell the right story?
Imagine six snack cards scattered on a canteen desk.
Some say apple with a capital letter and one uses a small letter.
Sorting the cards should help us understand the votes, but a computer may need us to use a consistent spelling first.
Good displays begin with careful checking.
Today we are learning to turn checked responses into a trustworthy frequency display.
Our goal is to turn responses into a trustworthy frequency table and display.
We are looking for a process someone else could follow and check.
A beautiful graph is not useful if the counts came from missing, mistaken or double-counted records.
I can spot missing, invalid and repeated records.
I can make a frequency table that counts every valid response once.
I can use a digital table or spreadsheet to represent data.
You already know how to sort objects into groups and count each group.
Today each card will represent one pupil’s response.
Think of the table as a tidy record of those groups.
Each response must contribute exactly once, and the total gives us an important check.
Frequency means how often a category or value occurs.
Validate means check the data against the question and collection rules before counting.
Use a consistent spelling, check missing answers with the collector, and investigate duplicate pupil records.
Matching answers from different pupils are not duplicates.
Never quietly invent a missing answer.
Collecting data and checking data are connected jobs.
First agree what choices are allowed and what one record represents.
Then look for unexpected words, empty spaces and repeated pupil records.
If a response is unclear, ask the collector or pupil to check it.
We must not guess which snack a blank answer meant.
Six different pupils answered: Apple, Banana, apple, Pear, Apple, Banana.
How many valid votes are there?
Look at the six cards before we sort them.
Predict the total number of votes.
Then look for cards that belong to the same snack group.
Take a moment to explain why matching snack choices from different pupils should still remain in our collection.
Standardise apple to Apple: Apple 3, Banana 2, Pear 1.
The total is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
All six votes count; repeated snack choices are normal.
Place the first Apple card in its group, then add the small-letter apple and the final Apple.
That group has three cards.
Banana has two and Pear has one.
Write those frequencies beside their labels.
Adding three, two and one gives six, matching the number of pupil responses we started with.
Put one vote in each cell A2 to A7.
In C2 type Apple.
What does =COUNTIF(A2:A7,C2) find?
Imagine moving the cards into a spreadsheet, one checked vote per row.
Put the category Apple in a separate cell.
Before using a counting tool, predict the number it should return.
What would you check if the result were different from the three Apple cards you sorted?
It counts the cells matching Apple.
Use a row for each category and check that the frequencies sum to six.
A column graph has separated equal-width bars, category labels and a frequency scale starting at zero.
The spreadsheet’s count-if formula counts the cells matching a chosen category.
It can help make the frequency table, but we still need to check spelling and the selected range of cells.
To draw a column graph, use one separated column for each snack.
Start the frequency scale at zero, label the categories, and use equal intervals.
Draw Apple’s column to three pupils, Banana’s column to two pupils and Pear’s column to one pupil.
“Remove every repeated answer.” Only repeated records for the same pupil need checking.
Different pupils may choose the same snack.
If two pupils both choose Banana, that is useful information about the class.
Removing one would change the evidence.
If the same pupil record appears twice, investigate whether it is a recording mistake.
The response value and the record identity answer different questions, so they need different checks.
